source_text: Denique quid exhortatio ipsius teneret, ostendit, praemittens: Humanum est quod dico, propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae; sicut enim exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiae et iniquitati ad iniquitatem; ita nunc exhibete membra vestra servire iustitiae in sanctificationem; cum enim servi essetis peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiae [n291] . Ordinatissime prorsus ipsos dicit liberos fuisse iustitiae, quos convenerat, ut membra sua in omni sanctificatione retinerent. Verum, quia non parum hic immorati sumus, ut ostenderemus certissimum esse quod dixeram [n292] , quia negarent liberum arbitrium homines qui vestro fuissent sermone deterriti, et in verum exitium vana formidine truderentur; atque te esse praecipuum arbitrii liberi negatorem; revertamur ad illum librum, qui est ad Valerium destinatus, ut probemus primo te negasse conditorem Deum; nunc autem, alibi quidem negare, alibi scelestius multo quam negaveras confiteri. Et quidem, quam in illo libro tuo priore absolute Deum negaveris conditorem hominum, satis cum discuteretur apparuit; dixisti quippe, quod genus humanum diabolus quasi plantati a se fruticis fructum iure decerperet [n293] ; multaque alia quae loco a te argumentorum posita huic cooperantur errori. In hoc vero secundo libro, etsi universitate dogmatis tui idem agas, tamen perniciosius niteris emendare sententiam, quam ante protulisti.
pass_a_gloss: Finally what the exhortation itself was holding, he showed, sending ahead: It is human what I say, on account of the infirmity of your flesh; for as you exhibited your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity; so now exhibit your members to serve justice unto sanctification; for when you were slaves of sin, you were free of justice. Most ordinately outright he says those themselves had been free of justice, whom he had convened, that they retain their members in all sanctification. But, because we have lingered here not a little, that we might show it most certain which I had said, that humans would deny free choice who had been deterred by your speech, and would be thrust by vain fear into true destruction; and that you are the chief denier of free choice; let us return to that book, which was destined to Valerius, that we may prove first that you denied God the founder; now however, elsewhere indeed to deny, elsewhere far more criminally than you had denied to confess. And indeed, how in that earlier book of yours you absolutely denied God the founder of humans, appeared enough when it was being shaken out; you said indeed, that the devil as if the fruit of a shrub planted by himself would by right pluck the human race; and many other things which placed by you in the place of arguments cooperate with this error. But in this second book, even if by the universe of your dogma you drive the same, nevertheless more perniciously you strive to emend a sentence, which you had brought forth before.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: He shows what his exhortation contains by saying first: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present your members to serve righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:19–20). With perfect consistency he says that those whom he had urged to keep their members in complete sanctification had been free from righteousness.

We have spent no little time here proving the complete certainty of what I said earlier in section 73: people terrified by your speech would deny free choice and be driven by empty fear into real destruction; and you are the chief denier of free choice. Let us therefore return to the book addressed to Valerius, to prove that at first you denied God as Creator, while now you deny him in some places and in others acknowledge him far more wickedly than you denied him. How absolutely you denied God as humanity's Creator in that earlier book of yours became sufficiently clear when it was examined. You said that the devil rightly plucked the human race like the fruit of a shrub he himself had planted (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 1.26). You added many other things, offered as arguments, that support this error. In this second book, although your doctrine as a whole pursues the same course, you attempt to amend your former statement in a more destructive way.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
